football_evidence.question: Can San Diego State contain Colorado State’s explosive runs?
football_evidence.assessment: Some measured evidence supports EdgeDesk’s lean toward San Diego State, and its own breakdown accounts for about 0.0 of the 3.6 points, but not the full gap. It is a research question, not a bet.
supporting: When San Diego State has the ball (the run game against the run defense): San Diego State’s offense averages 4.5 yards per carry, and Colorado State’s defense allows 8.0 yards per carry (FBS average 5.1).

When San Diego State has the ball (big plays through the air): San Diego State’s offense turns 8.7% of its pass plays into explosive gains, and Colorado State’s defense gives up explosive gains on 18.1% of opponent pass plays (FBS average 10.3%).

When San Diego State has the ball (big plays on the ground): San Diego State’s offense turns 3.7% of its runs into explosive gains, and Colorado State’s defense gives up explosive gains on 14.1% of opponent runs (FBS average 6.6%).

When Colorado State has the ball (big plays on the ground): Colorado State’s offense turns 7.8% of its runs into explosive gains, and San Diego State’s defense gives up explosive gains on 3.7% of opponent runs (FBS average 6.6%).
contradicting: When Colorado State has the ball (pass protection against the pass rush): Colorado State’s offense has allowed a sack on 1.3% of its dropbacks, and San Diego State’s defense sacks the quarterback on 6.6% of opponent dropbacks (FBS average 5.6%).

When Colorado State has the ball (the red zone): Colorado State’s offense succeeds on 55.4% of its red-zone plays, and San Diego State’s defense allows success on 52.6% of opponent red-zone plays (FBS average 43.6%).

When Colorado State has the ball (the line of scrimmage on running plays): Colorado State’s offense is stopped at or behind the line on 18.3% of its runs, and San Diego State’s defense stops 9.7% of opponent runs at or behind the line (FBS average 17.4%).
